title: "Showdowns"
body-classes: fam-cross
---

[**Cross-method**]{.fam-badge} · two head-to-head bake-offs on the course's own [common datasets](../phase0/concept_inventory.md) — same data, same split, many models — so the *differences between methods* (not the dataset) are what you read. The **classification showdown** lines up [Logistic Regression](../methods/logistic.qmd), [LDA](../methods/lda.qmd), [kNN](../methods/knn.qmd), a [Decision Tree](../methods/decision_trees.qmd) and a [Random Forest](../methods/random_forests.qmd) on a shared 2-D boundary; the **regression showdown** lines up [OLS](../methods/ols.qmd), [Ridge](../methods/regularization.qmd), [Lasso](../methods/regularization.qmd), a [Tree](../methods/decision_trees.qmd) and a [Random Forest](../methods/random_forests.qmd) on Hitters. Every number on this page is **computed in the course `.venv`** — no values are transcribed by hand.

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
**Why a showdown earns its place.** Each method page argues *in isolation* why its model draws the boundary or fits the curve it does. A showdown puts them on the **same canvas**: with Age and Fare held fixed, the *only* thing that changes between the five panels below is the **inductive bias of the model** — so you can literally see linear-vs-wiggly-vs-staircase side by side. The [decision dashboard](decision_dashboard.qmd) turns these observations into a "which model when?" guide; this page is the empirical evidence behind it.
:::

## 1. Classification showdown — five decision boundaries on one 2-D dataset {#sec-clf-showdown}

The setup is deliberately minimal so the boundary *shape* is the whole story. We load the Titanic training set, keep the two numeric features **Age** and **Fare** (dropping rows missing either — **714 of 891 rows survive**), and predict `Survived`. Five classifiers are fit on the standardized features, then asked to predict the class at every point of a coarse **40×40 grid** spanning the Age/Fare range; colouring the grid by predicted class draws each model's decision region *(all computed via `./.venv/Scripts/python.exe`, fixed `random_state=1`)*:

```python
sub = pd.read_csv("course_materials/Data/Titanic data/train.csv")[["Age","Fare","Survived"]].dropna()  # 891 → 714
X, y = sub[["Age","Fare"]].values, sub["Survived"].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)                       # scale so kNN distance is fair
models = {
    "Logistic":   LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    "LDA":        LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(),
    "kNN (k=15)": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15),
    "Tree (d=3)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=1),
    "RF (d=3)":   RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, random_state=1),
}
```

The in-sample (training-set) accuracies are close — the two features alone are weak predictors of survival, so this is a *boundary-shape* comparison, **not** a leaderboard — *(computed)*:

| Model | [Logistic](../methods/logistic.qmd) | [LDA](../methods/lda.qmd) | [kNN (k=15)](../methods/knn.qmd) | [Tree (d=3)](../methods/decision_trees.qmd) | [RF (d=3)](../methods/random_forests.qmd) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Train accuracy | 0.657 | 0.647 | 0.712 | 0.707 | 0.716 |

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**These are *training* accuracies, reported only to show the boundaries are non-trivial — do not read them as a model ranking.** Age + Fare are two weak features (the strong Titanic signal is `Sex`/`Pclass`, dropped here on purpose), so all five sit near the ~0.59 base rate's modest improvement. The kNN/Tree/RF edge is partly the flexible models tracing training points more closely — exactly the variance the [bias–variance](../methods/bias_variance.qmd) lens warns about. The point of this panel is the *geometry*, not the accuracy. The [kNN](../methods/knn.qmd) block ships as a comparison here but is a **Tier-2 method** in the build; treat its panel as illustrative of "non-parametric wiggle," not as an exam-ready recipe.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-clf-boundaries
//| fig-cap: "Decision-boundary showdown: five classifiers on Titanic Age (x) vs Fare (y), predicting Survived, computed via the course .venv (714 rows, StandardScaler, 40×40 grid, random_state=1). Each panel shades the grid by the model's predicted class (lilac = predicted survived, pale grey = predicted died); the dots are a 180-point subsample of the actual passengers (dark = survived, light = died). What to notice: Logistic and LDA draw a single straight line (a tilted half-plane) — the linear family; kNN(15) carves an irregular, locally-wiggly region that follows clumps of points; the depth-3 Tree partitions into a few axis-aligned rectangular blocks (perpendicular cuts only); and the Random Forest, averaging 100 such shallow trees, softens those steps into a smoother blocky region. Same data, same axes — the only thing changing is each model's inductive bias."

famCross  = (getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--family-cross').trim()  || "#3D405B")

:39.0,"fare":83.16,"s":1},{"age":32.0,"fare":7.85,"s":1},{"age":19.0,"fare":91.08,"s":1},{"age":22.0,"fare":9.0,"s":0},{"age":58.0,"fare":29.7,"s":0},{"age":19.0,"fare":26.0,"s":1},{"age":18.0,"fare":18.0,"s":0},{"age":24.0,"fare":14.5,"s":1},{"age":4.0,"fare":81.86,"s":1},{"age":22.0,"fare":29.0,"s":1},{"age":52.0,"fare":13.0,"s":0},{"age":20.0,"fare":9.85,"s":0},{"age":36.0,"fare":10.5,"s":0},{"age":35.0,"fare":10.5,"s":0}]})

// reshape grid into long form for faceting; grid is row-major with fare as outer loop, age as inner
clfModels = ["Logistic", "LDA", "kNN (k=15)", "Tree (d=3)", "RF (d=3)"]
clfGridLong = {
  const G = CLFOBJ.grid, age = CLFOBJ.ageLin, fare = CLFOBJ.fareLin;
  const out = [];
  for (const m of clfModels) {
    const b = CLFOBJ.boundary[m];
    for (let fi = 0; fi < G; fi++) {
      for (let ai = 0; ai < G; ai++) {
        out.push({model: m, age: age[ai], fare: fare[fi], pred: b[fi*G + ai]});
      }
    }
  }
  return out;
}
clfScatterAll = clfModels.flatMap(m => CLFOBJ.scatter.map(d => ({...d, model: m})))

Plot.plot({
  height: 260,
  marginLeft: 48,
  width: 900,
  grid: false,
  facet: {data: clfGridLong, x: "model"},
  fx: {label: null, domain: clfModels},
  x: {label: "Age →", domain: CLFOBJ.ageRange},
  y: {label: "Fare →", domain: [0, 160]},   // clip extreme fares so boundaries are legible
  color: {type: "ordinal", domain: [0, 1], range: ["#e9e9ee", famCross], legend: false},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(clfGridLong, {fx: "model", x: "age", y: "fare", fill: "pred", interval: undefined, inset: -0.5, fillOpacity: 0.55}),
    Plot.dot(clfScatterAll.filter(d => d.s === 1), {fx: "model", x: "age", y: "fare", r: 1.7, fill: famLinear, fillOpacity: 0.85}),
    Plot.dot(clfScatterAll.filter(d => d.s === 0), {fx: "model", x: "age", y: "fare", r: 1.7, fill: "#b9772b", fillOpacity: 0.55})
  ]
})
```

**Reading it — linear vs local vs axis-aligned.** The two **linear-family** classifiers, [Logistic Regression](../methods/logistic.qmd) and [LDA](../methods/lda.qmd), produce a *single straight cut* across the plane — exactly what their §1/§2 promise: both place a hyperplane, differing only in *how* (logistic fits the log-odds directly; LDA assumes Gaussian classes with a shared covariance and gets a line as a consequence, [LDA §8](../methods/lda.qmd#sec-lda-math)). Here they tilt almost identically, the textbook "on data where LDA's assumptions roughly hold, the two land in the same neighbourhood" ([logistic §6](../methods/logistic.qmd), [LDA §4](../methods/lda.qmd#sec-lda-toy)). Neither can bend: if survival depended on Age and Fare in a curved way, both would underfit it the same way.

[**kNN (k=15)**](../methods/knn.qmd) is the visible opposite. Its region is **irregular and locally wiggly** — pockets of "survived" appear wherever a cluster of survivors sits, because each grid cell is labelled by a majority vote of its 15 nearest training points. This is the non-parametric flexibility kNN §1 advertises ("it can carve out arbitrarily wiggly decision boundaries") and the variance kNN §2 warns about: with a smaller `k` the region would fragment further; with a much larger `k` it would smooth toward the global majority. It draws no global rule — only "who is nearby."

The two **tree-family** models show the third geometry: **axis-aligned steps**. The single depth-3 [Decision Tree](../methods/decision_trees.qmd) partitions the plane into a handful of rectangular blocks with perpendicular edges — never a diagonal — because every split is a threshold on one feature at a time ([decision-trees §1](../methods/decision_trees.qmd): "staircase boundaries… perpendicular cuts"). The depth-3 [Random Forest](../methods/random_forests.qmd) averages 100 such shallow trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample with a random feature subset, so its boundary is a *smoother, finer* version of the same blocky shape — the [variance reduction of §1](../methods/random_forests.qmd) made visible: the jagged single-tree steps soften into a more stable region without ever becoming a smooth curve. A tree wins when the true boundary is blocky; it pays a jagged-staircase tax when the truth is a clean diagonal — which is exactly the trade the [decision dashboard](decision_dashboard.qmd) encodes.

## 2. Regression showdown — five regressors on Hitters {#sec-reg-showdown}

The regression bake-off uses the Spring-2025 exam's first dataset, **`Hitters.csv`** (**263 players** after dropping missing salaries, **16 numeric predictors**, target `Salary` in \$1000s), with the canonical **75/25 split, `random_state=1`**, and a `StandardScaler` inside a pipeline for the linear models. This is the *same* setup as the [OLS](../methods/ols.qmd#sec-ols-hitters) and [regularization](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters) pages, extended with a Tree and a Forest *(all computed via `./.venv/Scripts/python.exe`)*:

```python
hd = pd.read_csv("Hitters.csv").dropna(subset=["Salary"])     # 322 → 263
X = hd.select_dtypes("number").drop(columns=["Salary"]); y = hd["Salary"]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X.values, y.values, test_size=0.25, random_state=1)
models = {
    "OLS":        make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()),
    "RidgeCV":    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3,3,100))),
    "LassoCV":    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=10, max_iter=100000, random_state=1)),
    "Tree (d=3)": DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=1),
    "RF (d=3)":   RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, random_state=1),
}
```

The computed test-set metrics — the headline of the showdown:

| Model | Train $R^2$ | **Test $R^2$** | Test RMSE (\$k) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [OLS](../methods/ols.qmd#sec-ols-hitters) | 0.55 | 0.36 | 377 |
| [Ridge (CV)](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters) | 0.54 | 0.39 | 370 |
| [Lasso (CV)](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters) | 0.54 | 0.38 | 373 |
| [Tree (d=3)](../methods/decision_trees.qmd) | 0.74 | 0.37 | 375 |
| [RF (d=3)](../methods/random_forests.qmd) | **0.79** | **0.59** | **304** |

*(All values computed; the OLS/Ridge/Lasso rows reproduce the [OLS](../methods/ols.qmd#sec-ols-hitters) and [regularization](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters) pages to the digit.)*

**Reading it — OLS overfits, shrinkage helps a little, the forest helps a lot.** Plain [**OLS**](../methods/ols.qmd#sec-ols-hitters) is the weakest of the five: **test $R^2 = 0.36$** against a **train $R^2 = 0.55$**, the wide train–test gap that is the *fingerprint of variance* ([OLS §4](../methods/ols.qmd#sec-ols-hitters), [§6](../methods/ols.qmd)). The cause is structural — 16 partly-redundant career totals (`CAtBat`, `CHits`, `CRuns`… all move together), so OLS fits the training sample's noise. This is precisely the diagnosis the OLS page makes and the cue it hands to regularization.

[**Ridge**](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters) and [**Lasso**](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters), with cross-validated `alpha`, do exactly what [regularization §4](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-hitters) predicts: they trade a little training fit (train $R^2$ 0.55 → 0.54) for better generalization (**test $R^2$ 0.36 → 0.38–0.39**, RMSE 377 → 370–373). The gain is *modest but real* — the bias–variance trade-off made concrete, and the reasoning the exam grades. Note that a penalty cannot fix a *wrong functional form*: if the Salary surface is genuinely non-linear, shrinking linear coefficients only goes so far ([regularization §2](../methods/regularization.qmd#sec-reg-when): "a penalty cannot fix a wrong functional form").

The two **tree-family** models bracket the lesson. A *single* depth-3 [**Tree**](../methods/decision_trees.qmd) reaches **test $R^2 = 0.37$** — no better than OLS — while its train $R^2$ (0.74) already shows the high-variance, memorize-the-sample behaviour [decision-trees §1/§5](../methods/decision_trees.qmd#sec-tree-viz) describes; "a single tree's variance can't be cross-validated away, only ensembled away." And that is exactly what the depth-3 [**Random Forest**](../methods/random_forests.qmd) does: averaging 100 decorrelated shallow trees lifts **test $R^2$ to 0.59 and cuts RMSE to \$304k** — comfortably the best model here. It captures the non-linear, interaction-heavy structure the linear models cannot, while the bagging-plus-feature-randomness of [random-forests §1](../methods/random_forests.qmd) controls the variance a lone tree cannot. The ordering — RF ≫ Ridge ≈ Lasso > Tree ≈ OLS — is the cross-method story in one line: **when the truth is non-linear with redundant predictors, an ensemble of shallow trees beats both the linear baseline and its regularized fixes.**

::: {.callout-exam}
**How a showdown maps to the exam.** The Spring-2025 take-home runs these comparisons *separately* — Assignment 1 is OLS-vs-Ridge-vs-Lasso on Hitters (the left three bars), Assignment 3 is Tree-vs-Random-Forest-vs-boosting on WDBC. This page puts the regression contenders on one axis to make the *relative* gains legible: the marks reward (i) diagnosing OLS's variance from the train–test gap, (ii) justifying why shrinkage narrows it, and (iii) explaining why a non-linear ensemble can leap past *all* the linear models when the relationship isn't linear. See the [decision dashboard](decision_dashboard.qmd) for the "which model when" summary and each method page's §7 for the per-assignment detail.
:::

## 3. What the two showdowns share {#sec-takeaway}

Both panels are the same idea told twice. In **classification**, model choice changes the *shape* of the boundary — linear (Logistic/LDA), local-wiggly (kNN), or axis-aligned-blocky (Tree/RF) — and the right choice depends on the true boundary's geometry. In **regression**, model choice changes how the bias–variance budget is spent — OLS pays in variance, Ridge/Lasso buy it back with a little bias, a single Tree overfits, and the Forest spends its budget on *decorrelated averaging* to win. The unifying lens is [bias–variance](../methods/bias_variance.qmd), and the practical "pick one" guide is the [decision dashboard](decision_dashboard.qmd); every method's own §2 ("when to use / when not") is the per-model version of the same advice.
